Three deeper frames matter more:\n\n1. **The harness conflates plan gates with review gates.** The list of\n   bullets under `## Gate criteria (for the human reviewer)` in the M0\n   spec was written for a human reading a PR, and then reused verbatim\n   as the review criteria. Megaplan has no concept that a spec may carry\n   two audiences. The container runs with the human-facing list and is\n   then punished for being unable to satisfy it.\n2. **Spec authorship has no feedback loop.** Nothing in megaplan looks\n   at a spec before execution and asks \"are these criteria reachable by\n   the agent configured to execute this plan?\" The author pastes\n   best-practice gates from CLAUDE.md; megaplan dutifully hands them to\n   review; review dutifully fails. The error is diagnosed at the most\n   expensive possible moment — after a full execute pass in a remote\n   container.\n3. **The review agent already has a `waived` escape hatch and doesn't\n   use it aggressively.** `megaplan/prompts/review.py:503` instructs\n   review to mark criteria `waived` \"if a criterion cannot be verified\n   in this context (e.g., requires manual testing or runtime\n   observation)\". In the M0 run this path was not taken — the reviewer\n   treated \"cannot verify interaction counts\" as a `must` failure rather\n   than a waiver. So the mechanism exists but the contract is ambiguous:\n   unverifiable versus failed is a judgement call, with no structural\n   signal from the spec telling the reviewer which one applies.\n\nAny proposal that only addresses frame 1 will succeed on M0 and then\nfail on the next poorly-authored spec. A proposal that addresses all\nthree is a real fix.\n\n## Option space\n\n### (a) Per-criterion `verified_by: container|human|mixed` tag\nReviewer skips (waives) any criterion tagged `human` when running in an\nautonomous context. Small change: schema plus two lines of reviewer\nlogic. Catches: obvious human-only gates. Misses: the authorship problem\n(author has to remember to tag; no enforcement), the dual-audience\nproblem (still one criteria list), the expensive-machine-gate problem\n(e2e suites are neither human nor container-easy). Low implementation\ncost; zero worker-contract change; fully backward compatible (missing\ntag = `container` default).\n\n### (b) Plan-phase verifiability audit\nBefore critique starts, the harness runs a lightweight check — most\ncheaply a single worker call — that inspects each proposed success\ncriterion and emits a flag if the criterion is unreachable by the\nconfigured worker. Catches: bad authorship early, when it is cheap to\nfix. Misses: criteria that look machine-verifiable but aren't (dev-only\ntelemetry, flaky e2e). Medium cost; requires a new prompt and a new\nflag category; plays well with the existing critique→gate loop because\nthe flags become part of normal resolution. Does not require a schema\nchange if we keep it advisory.\n\n### (c) Deferred-verification terminal state\nAdd a plan state `awaiting_human_verification` distinct from `done`.\nHuman-tagged criteria short-circuit the review `needs_rework` verdict\nand instead park the plan in this state; a human CLI command\n(`megaplan verify-human --plan X --criterion C --pass`) flips it to\n`done`. Catches: the end-to-end lifecycle including \"who actually\nconfirmed\". Misses: still requires the tagging from (a) upstream; adds\na new state machine branch that has to be taught to status, batch\nrunners, and loop-init. Medium-to-large cost; meaningful worker\ncontract change (review must emit a new verdict `awaiting_human` in\naddition to `approved` / `needs_rework`).\n\n### (d) Two-array schema split (machine_criteria, human_criteria)\nThe plan author writes two explicit arrays. Review evaluates only\n`machine_criteria`. `human_criteria` go into the PR description or a\nchecklist file and never touch review. Catches: the conflation directly\nat the schema level; makes the author's two audiences structurally\nseparate. Misses: authors who lazily shove everything into one bucket;\nthe expensive-machine-gate case. Small cost; but a large change in\nauthoring ergonomics — existing specs break unless we fall back to\ntreating `success_criteria` as `machine_criteria`.\n\n### (e) Reviewer self-assessment of verifiability\nLet the reviewer return, per criterion, one of\n`pass | fail | waived_unverifiable | waived_info`. Today's `waived`\ncovers both `info` priority and unverifiable; split that. The reviewer\ndecides, not the author. Catches: the M0 case without touching spec\nauthoring; the reviewer is usually in the best position to know what\nit cannot verify. Misses: authors still paste nonsense criteria; the\nloop wastes a whole execute pass before the reviewer shrugs; also\ncreates a new gaming vector where `waived_unverifiable` means \"I didn't\ntry hard enough.\" Low cost in isolation.\n\n### (f) Worker capability profile + static criterion linter\nNew-for-this-proposal. Each worker declares a *capability profile* — a\nsmall structured blob listing what it can execute (`run_shell`,\n`run_node_tests`, `read_build_output`, `observe_browser`,\n`observe_runtime_logs`, ...). At plan-finalize time, each success\ncriterion is parsed by a linter prompt that maps it to the capabilities\nit needs. A criterion whose required capabilities are a subset of the\nconfigured worker's profile is `machine_verifiable: true`. Everything\nelse is `machine_verifiable: false` and is automatically treated as a\nhuman-deferred criterion. The author does not tag anything; the\nharness computes it.\n\n## Recommendation: a fused (a)+(b)+(e), with (f) as the v0.18 follow-up\n\nPick option (a) as the storage model, option (b) as the upstream defense,\nand option (e) as the downstream safety net. Deliver all three in v0.17.0.\nDefer (f) because capability profiles are a much bigger design problem —\nthey couple to worker contracts, the trusted-container env, and the\nhermes worker, and we do not need them to fix the immediate pain. (c) is\ntempting but adds a state machine branch for a problem that `waived`\nalready models well; reject. (d) forces existing specs to break; reject.\n\nWhy fuse three rather than pick one: each option on its own has a\nfailure mode the other two cover.\n\n- (a) alone: author forgets to tag -> reviewer still fails. (e) catches.\n- (b) alone: audit passes because criteria *look* machine-verifiable\n  (e.g., \"baseline counts captured\" reads as machine-checkable but\n  requires a browser). (a) plus (e) catch at review time.\n- (e) alone: reviewer correctly waives, but the author never learns\n  the spec was malformed; the next milestone repeats the mistake. (b)\n  surfaces the problem at authorship.\n\nThe three-layer structure mirrors megaplan's existing philosophy (plan\ngate filters → execute audit → review verdict), just applied to the\nverifiability axis.\n\n## Implementation sketch\n\n### Schema changes (`megaplan/schemas.py`)\n`plan.json` and `finalize.json` success_criteria items gain:\n```\n\"verified_by\": {\"type\": \"string\", \"enum\": [\"container\", \"human\", \"mixed\"], \"default\": \"container\"}\n\"verification_hint\": {\"type\": \"string\"}  // optional, free-text: \"requires running browser\", etc.\n```\nReview-output criteria gain a new `pass` enum value:\n```\n\"pass\": {\"type\": \"string\", \"enum\": [\"pass\", \"fail\", \"waived\", \"waived_unverifiable\", \"deferred_human\"]}\n```\nExisting `waived` is preserved for `info` priority. Missing `verified_by`\ndefaults to `container` — every existing plan keeps working unchanged.\n\n### Plan-phase audit (option b)\nNew file: `megaplan/verifiability.py`. Exposes `audit_criteria(state, criteria)`\nwhich runs a single-shot worker call (same pattern as `run_gate_checks`)\nasking: \"for each criterion, is it reachable by a worker with capabilities\n`run_shell`, `read_files`, `git`, but no browser, no human hands, no manual\nobservation? Return `container`, `human`, or `mixed` and one-line\nrationale.\" Results are written to `plan_dir/verifiability.json` and\nsurfaced as advisory critique flags with category `verifiability`. The\nauthor (or gate) can override by explicitly setting `verified_by` on the\ncriterion — the audit never overwrites an explicit tag, only fills in\nmissing ones.\n\nRuns after `finalize`, before `execute` starts. Keeps the\ncritique→gate→revise loop as the resolution surface — no new state.\n\n### Review-phase handling (option e)\n`megaplan/prompts/review.py` gains two rules:\n- If criterion's `verified_by == \"human\"`: reviewer MUST mark\n  `pass: \"deferred_human\"` and MUST NOT count it toward the\n  `needs_rework` tally. `review_verdict = approved` is valid even if\n  every human criterion is deferred.\n- If reviewer finds a `container`-tagged criterion it genuinely cannot\n  verify (e.g., the tooling isn't present in this environment), it\n  marks `pass: \"waived_unverifiable\"` with an evidence sentence naming\n  *what* it couldn't run, and surfaces a flag `REVIEW-UNVERIFIABLE-NNN`.\n  A `must` criterion going `waived_unverifiable` is a soft block — it\n  downgrades verdict to `needs_rework` only if `>= N` of them occur\n  (configurable; default 1 for `must`, infinity for `should`). This\n  prevents the M0 cascade.\n\nMerging logic (`_merge_review_verdicts` at `handlers.py:1421`) must learn\nthe new enum values and stop treating them as `fail`.\n\n### CLI\n- `megaplan audit-verifiability --plan X` — run the audit on demand.\n- `megaplan status` shows counts: \"3 container / 2 human / 0 mixed\".\n- `megaplan verify-human --plan X --criterion \"Baseline doc captured\"\n  --pass --evidence \"Confirmed 5 components × 3 interactions in doc\n  at commit abc123\"` — records the human confirmation in\n  `plan_dir/human_verifications.json`. Review re-runs treat these as\n  resolved. (Optional for v0.17.0; falls back to \"human flips state\n  with a comment\" if we want to defer.)\n\n### Migration\n- Existing plans without `verified_by`: default `container`. Same\n  behavior as today.\n- Existing plans in `awaiting_review` / `needs_rework` for the M0-class\n  reason: add a one-shot retrofit script that parses the review verdict\n  and re-tags criteria whose failure evidence includes phrases like\n  \"cannot verify\", \"no browser\", \"requires manual\". Offered as a CLI\n  tool, not automatic.\n- Tests: add fixtures under `tests/fixtures/verifiability/` that mirror\n  M0 — container-only execution, spec with mixed gates, expected\n  `approved` verdict with deferrals.\n\n### Out of scope (v0.17.0)\n- Worker capability profiles (option f). Deferred to v0.18.0 when we\n  re-examine worker contracts wholesale.\n- Schema-level split into two arrays (option d). Tag is sufficient.\n- Auto-flipping `awaiting_human_verification` based on PR comments or\n  GitHub checks. Manual CLI confirmation only.\n- Teaching loop mode about deferrals. v0.17.0 treats a plan with any\n  `deferred_human` criteria as \"done for autonomous purposes\"; loops\n  continue to the next plan.\n\n## Success criteria (verifiable)\n\n- `megaplan init` accepts plans whose `success_criteria[].verified_by`\n  is `container`, `human`, or `mixed`. Missing field defaults to\n  `container` — asserted by schema round-trip test.\n- `megaplan audit-verifiability --plan X` produces\n  `verifiability.json` with one entry per criterion and exits 0.\n- A fixture plan with a `verified_by: human` criterion runs through\n  review and yields `review_verdict: approved`, `pass: deferred_human`\n  for that criterion, and no `rework_items` entries sourced from it.\n- A fixture plan with an undetectable-by-container criterion (e.g.,\n  \"browser renders without warnings\") and `verified_by` unset triggers\n  a verifiability flag at audit time, category `verifiability`.\n- Reviewer emitting `pass: waived_unverifiable` on a `must` criterion\n  still routes to `needs_rework` (soft block preserved); emitting it\n  on a `should` criterion does not.\n- `megaplan verify-human --plan X --criterion C --pass --evidence E`\n  writes `human_verifications.json` and, on a re-review, the entry is\n  honored: verdict stays `approved`, pass flips from `deferred_human`\n  to `pass`.\n- Existing test suite passes unchanged — all legacy plans default to\n  `container` and behave exactly as before.\n- `pyproject.toml` version is `0.17.0`; CHANGELOG has the v0.17.0 entry.\n\n## Edge cases — and answers\n\n- **Mixed human + machine gates in one plan.** Supported first-class;\n  review emits both `pass` and `deferred_human` verdicts; `approved` is\n  possible when all machine `must` criteria pass and all human `must`\n  criteria are deferred. The plan status becomes `approved_with_deferrals`\n  in `status` output — a label, not a new state.\n- **Worker identity changes mid-plan** (claude plans, codex executes,\n  hermes reviews). Capability is conservatively the intersection across\n  the executing + reviewing workers. The audit runs with the *executor's*\n  profile; review with its own. If review has fewer capabilities than\n  execute, `waived_unverifiable` can still fire at review time — this is\n  correct: review couldn't verify, regardless of whether execute could.\n- **Machine-verifiable but expensive** (full e2e, 30-minute build).\n  These are `verified_by: container` but get a `verification_hint` of\n  `\"expensive\"`. Not handled in v0.17.0 — a future `verified_by: container_slow`\n  tag would let the harness choose to defer them in CI-gated contexts.\n  Explicitly out of scope now; the hint is present so we do not have to\n  re-migrate schemas later.\n- **Gaming: author marks everything `human` to skip checks.** Three\n  defenses. (1) The verifiability audit runs regardless of the author's\n  tag; if the audit says a criterion *is* container-reachable, that\n  appears as a flag at gate time even when the author claimed `human`.\n  (2) `megaplan status` surfaces the container/human ratio; a plan with\n  7 human and 0 container criteria is visually anomalous to the human\n  operator. (3) Review's `waived_unverifiable` counter still applies —\n  marking something `human` does not exempt it from the soft block if\n  review independently finds the claim is machine-checkable. We do not\n  try to make gaming impossible; we make it visible.\n\n## Authorship ergonomics\n\nToday a spec author writes one list of bullets. Under v0.17.0 they write\nthe same list, and most criteria default to `container` implicitly. The\nonly new burden is tagging the criteria they already know a machine\ncannot verify. To lower even that burden:\n\n- The `megaplan init` prompt gains a one-line nudge: \"Any success\n  criterion that requires human observation (browser, device, QA\n  confirmation) should set `verified_by: human`.\"\n- A scaffolding command `megaplan new-spec --template milestone` writes\n  a template markdown file with two example criteria pre-filled, one\n  per `verified_by` value, so the author sees the shape.\n- The verifiability audit's output is itself the teaching signal: if\n  the author forgets, the flag surfaces with rationale and the author\n  learns the pattern on the next spec.\n\nThe system is strictly *easier* to get right: the failure mode goes\nfrom \"ship to a container, burn a run, fail review opaquely\" to\n\"critique emits a flag at plan time, author adjusts tag or rewrites\ncriterion.\" The only way v0.17.0 is harder than today is if the author\nwants to preserve the current behavior of pasting CLAUDE.md bullets\ninto the criteria block — which is exactly the behavior we are trying\nto make uncomfortable.\n\n## Branch\n`gate-verifiability` off main.\n\n## Working directory\n/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/megaplan\n"

#!/bin/bash
# Chain next milestone once current one finishes.
# Polls plan status; on terminal `done` state, inits + runs the next plan.
# On failure terminal states (aborted/escalated/stalled), stops cleanly.

set -u

LOG=/workspace/chain.log
exec > >(tee -a "$LOG") 2>&1

log() { echo "[chain $(date -Iseconds)] $*"; }

wait_for_plan_done() {
  local plan="$1"
  local last_state=""
  local same_state_count=0
  local max_stall_polls=180  # 180 × 60s = 3h without state change → bail (execute can take 1-2h between state transitions)

  while true; do
    local state
    state=$(cd /workspace/reigh-app && megaplan status --plan "$plan" 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.state // "missing"')

    case "$state" in
      done)
        log "plan $plan reached done"
        return 0
        ;;
      aborted|failed|escalated)
        log "plan $plan ended in terminal-failure state: $state — chain stops"
        return 1
        ;;
      missing)
        log "plan $plan not found (may have been wiped); chain stops"
        return 1
        ;;
      *)
        if [[ "$state" == "$last_state" ]]; then
          same_state_count=$((same_state_count + 1))
          if [[ $same_state_count -ge $max_stall_polls ]]; then
            log "plan $plan stuck at state=$state for $max_stall_polls polls (~$((max_stall_polls))m) — chain stops"
            return 1
          fi
        else
          same_state_count=0
          last_state="$state"
          log "plan $plan state: $state"
        fi
        sleep 60
        ;;
    esac
  done
}

init_and_run() {
  local idea_path="$1"
  local label="$2"

  log "initializing $label plan from $idea_path"
  cd /workspace/reigh-app || { log "repo missing"; return 1; }

  # Refresh main so the new plan branches from latest
  git fetch origin main 2>&1 | tail -2
  git checkout main 2>&1 | tail -2
  git pull --ff-only origin main 2>&1 | tail -2

  local init_output
  init_output=$(
    IDEA="$(cat "$idea_path")"
    megaplan init --project-dir /workspace/reigh-app --auto-approve --robustness standard "$IDEA" 2>&1
  )
  echo "$init_output" | tee /workspace/chain-init-$label.log | tail -10

  local new_plan
  new_plan=$(echo "$init_output" | jq -r '.plan // empty' 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ -z "$new_plan" ]]; then
    # Fallback: grep for the plan name
    new_plan=$(echo "$init_output" | grep -oE '"[a-z0-9-]+-[0-9]{8}-[0-9]{4}"' | head -1 | tr -d '"')
  fi

  if [[ -z "$new_plan" ]]; then
    log "could not extract plan name from init output — chain stops"
    return 1
  fi
  log "launched $label = $new_plan"
  echo "$new_plan" > /workspace/chain-current-plan.txt

  # Fire auto driver in its own supervised tmux session so it survives ssh
  # disconnects AND restarts on transient failures (network blips, etc).
  # Old: send-keys to the shared 'agent' tmux which ran auto bare.
  tmux kill-session -t exec 2>/dev/null || true
  mp-run exec mp-supervise "$new_plan" "$label" bash -c "cd /workspace/reigh-app && MEGAPLAN_TRUSTED_CONTAINER=1 megaplan auto --plan $new_plan --on-escalate fail --stall-threshold 5 --max-iterations 100 --phase-timeout 3600"
  echo "$new_plan"
}

# ---- Config: edit this to change the chain ----
CURRENT_PLAN="milestone-m0-from-docs-state-20260415-0217"

# Each entry: "label:idea-path"
NEXT_MILESTONES=(
  "m1:/workspace/ideas/M1-foundation-store.txt"
  "m1a:/workspace/ideas/M1a-settings-store.txt"
  "m1b:/workspace/ideas/M1b-selection-store.txt"
  "m1c:/workspace/ideas/M1c-timeline-store.txt"
  # M2 (overlay stack) is CONDITIONAL on M1a's gate — do NOT auto-queue.
)
# ----

log "chain watcher starting; current plan: $CURRENT_PLAN"

# Band-aid: ensure the seed plan is driven by megaplan auto under supervisor,
# the same way chained plans are. Without this, the seed has no state-aware
# driver and a needs_rework bounce can leave it stuck. Launch only if no exec
# session is already running for it.
seed_state=$(cd /workspace/reigh-app && megaplan status --plan "$CURRENT_PLAN" 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.state // "missing"')
if [[ "$seed_state" != "done" && "$seed_state" != "aborted" && "$seed_state" != "failed" && "$seed_state" != "missing" ]]; then
  if ! tmux has-session -t exec 2>/dev/null; then
    log "seed plan $CURRENT_PLAN state=$seed_state — launching megaplan auto under supervisor"
    mp-run exec mp-supervise "$CURRENT_PLAN" seed bash -c "cd /workspace/reigh-app && MEGAPLAN_TRUSTED_CONTAINER=1 megaplan auto --plan $CURRENT_PLAN --on-escalate fail --stall-threshold 5 --max-iterations 100 --phase-timeout 3600"
  else
    log "seed plan $CURRENT_PLAN: tmux 'exec' already running — assuming driver in place"
  fi
fi

if ! wait_for_plan_done "$CURRENT_PLAN"; then
  log "chain halted before reaching next milestone"
  exit 1
fi

for entry in "${NEXT_MILESTONES[@]}"; do
  label="${entry%%:*}"
  idea="${entry#*:}"

  if [[ ! -f "$idea" ]]; then
    log "idea file missing: $idea — chain stops"
    exit 1
  fi

  new_plan=$(init_and_run "$idea" "$label") || { log "$label init failed"; exit 1; }
  CURRENT_PLAN="$new_plan"

  if ! wait_for_plan_done "$CURRENT_PLAN"; then
    log "$label ended non-successfully — chain stops here"
    exit 1
  fi
done

log "all chained milestones complete"

The M0 failure is not just "spec had human-only gates" — it is three overlapping problems: megaplan conflates plan gates (for human PR reviewers) with review gates (for the harness); spec authorship has no feedback loop, so bad criteria are discovered only after a full remote execute burns; and the review prompt's existing `waived` escape hatch is under-specified, so the reviewer fails `must` criteria it could legitimately have waived.

The proposal fuses three defenses in v0.17.0 rather than picking one. **(a)** Add a `verified_by: container|human|mixed` tag on each success criterion (default `container` — backward compatible). **(b)** Add a post-finalize verifiability audit (`megaplan/verifiability.py`) that emits advisory flags when a criterion looks unreachable by the configured worker — catching bad specs cheaply at plan time. **(e)** Split reviewer's `waived` into `deferred_human` and `waived_unverifiable`, with a soft-block counter so a single unverifiable `must` still trips rework. Option (f) — full worker capability profiles — is deferred to v0.18.0. The doc includes schema fragments, CLI shape (`audit-verifiability`, `verify-human`), migration path, eight machine-verifiable success criteria, and explicit answers to the edge cases the prompt flagged (mixed gates, mid-plan worker swap, expensive-but-machine gates, gaming by over-tagging `human`).

## What to challenge

Go after the proposal, not the author. Everything is on the table:

- **Is the framing right?** The proposal says the failure is three overlapping problems (plan-gate/review-gate conflation, no spec authorship feedback loop, underspecified `waived`). Is that actually the root, or is it still a symptom? What's the real deepest cause?
- **Is the 3-part combination actually coherent?** Or is it a compromise that partially solves each concern without fully solving any? Would picking ONE lever cleanly beat stacking three?
- **What happens at the seams?** When verifiability audit (b) flags a criterion but author ignores the advisory, does the reviewer still catch it? When reviewer uses `deferred_human` (e), who ever comes back to verify? Is there a real workflow for humans to complete deferred gates, or does the system just accumulate them?
- **Does this actually solve M0's failure mode?** Walk through the M0 run under the proposed system: which criteria would be tagged what, would the audit catch them, would review skip them, would state transition to done? Or would something else break?
- **Is `verified_by` the right axis?** Maybe the axis should be "evidence type" (file in repo, test output, screenshot, human assertion) not "verifier capability." Consider alternatives.
- **Does gaming `human` for everything really get caught?** The proposal says a "soft-block counter so a single unverifiable `must` still trips rework" — but the author of the spec is the one choosing `human` vs `container`, and they can just mark everything `human`. The counter only helps if a reviewer independently detects the gaming. Does that actually work?
- **Mid-plan worker swap**: critique's answer. Is it right? What about claude-for-plan + codex-for-execute + human for verify — does the system reason correctly about this?
- **Migration cost**: for existing specs without tags, default-to-container is back-compat — but then every existing human-gate accidentally becomes a container-required fail. Or does it? Check.
- **Complexity cost**: three new subsystems (tag field, audit module, reviewer splits). That's a lot of surface area for a problem that might be solvable with a simpler fix. Propose a simpler fix if you can.
- **Perverse incentives**: what does this encourage spec authors to do? Write specs that are harder to blow up? Or write specs that have laxer gates?
- **Who actually uses this**: megaplan is run by a solo dev today. Does this proposal scale sensibly to a 1-person ops model, or does it assume a team with a dedicated human-verifier?
- **Is the deferral concept dangerous**: if `deferred_human` lands a plan in a "done-ish" state without human verification, is that worse than just failing the plan?

2	
3	## Motivation — and a warning against the obvious reading
4	
5	The proximate trigger for this proposal is milestone M0 of the reigh-app
6	state-management refactor (`~/Documents/reigh-megaplan-dev/ideas/M0-render-telemetry.txt`).
7	Codex, running autonomously in a Railway container, shipped the actual code
8	deliverables — hook, overlay, 11 instrumented components, branch
9	`megaplan/m0-render-telemetry` — and then review blocked `done` with four
10	failures: a spec required "≥5 components × ≥3 interactions" of *observed*
11	render counts (needs a browser); a spec required a "non-HMR production-built
12	dev server" baseline (Vite strips `import.meta.env.DEV`, making the spec
13	semantically self-contradictory); `npm test` had 4 order-dependent failures
14	(real, but not caused by the milestone); and the baseline doc's directory
15	was `.gitignore`'d so codex force-added it (flagged as scope creep).
16	
17	The obvious reading is "add a `verified_by: human` tag so the reviewer
18	skips those criteria in autonomous mode." That reading is too shallow and
19	this proposal will resist it. Three deeper frames matter more:
20	
21	1. **The harness conflates plan gates with review gates.** The list of
22	   bullets under `## Gate criteria (for the human reviewer)` in the M0
23	   spec was written for a human reading a PR, and then reused verbatim
24	   as the review criteria. Megaplan has no concept that a spec may carry
25	   two audiences. The container runs with the human-facing list and is
26	   then punished for being unable to satisfy it.
27	2. **Spec authorship has no feedback loop.** Nothing in megaplan looks
28	   at a spec before execution and asks "are these criteria reachable by
29	   the agent configured to execute this plan?" The author pastes
30	   best-practice gates from CLAUDE.md; megaplan dutifully hands them to
31	   review; review dutifully fails. The error is diagnosed at the most
32	   expensive possible moment — after a full execute pass in a remote
33	   container.
34	3. **The review agent already has a `waived` escape hatch and doesn't
35	   use it aggressively.** `megaplan/prompts/review.py:503` instructs
36	   review to mark criteria `waived` "if a criterion cannot be verified
37	   in this context (e.g., requires manual testing or runtime
38	   observation)". In the M0 run this path was not taken — the reviewer
39	   treated "cannot verify interaction counts" as a `must` failure rather
40	   than a waiver. So the mechanism exists but the contract is ambiguous:
41	   unverifiable versus failed is a judgement call, with no structural
42	   signal from the spec telling the reviewer which one applies.
43	
44	Any proposal that only addresses frame 1 will succeed on M0 and then
45	fail on the next poorly-authored spec. A proposal that addresses all
46	three is a real fix.
47	
48	## Option space
49	
50	### (a) Per-criterion `verified_by: container|human|mixed` tag
51	Reviewer skips (waives) any criterion tagged `human` when running in an
52	autonomous context. Small change: schema plus two lines of reviewer
53	logic. Catches: obvious human-only gates. Misses: the authorship problem
54	(author has to remember to tag; no enforcement), the dual-audience
55	problem (still one criteria list), the expensive-machine-gate problem
56	(e2e suites are neither human nor container-easy). Low implementation
57	cost; zero worker-contract change; fully backward compatible (missing
58	tag = `container` default).
59	
60	### (b) Plan-phase verifiability audit
61	Before critique starts, the harness runs a lightweight check — most
62	cheaply a single worker call — that inspects each proposed success
63	criterion and emits a flag if the criterion is unreachable by the
64	configured worker. Catches: bad authorship early, when it is cheap to
65	fix. Misses: criteria that look machine-verifiable but aren't (dev-only
66	telemetry, flaky e2e). Medium cost; requires a new prompt and a new
67	flag category; plays well with the existing critique→gate loop because
68	the flags become part of normal resolution. Does not require a schema
69	change if we keep it advisory.
70	
71	### (c) Deferred-verification terminal state
72	Add a plan state `awaiting_human_verification` distinct from `done`.
73	Human-tagged criteria short-circuit the review `needs_rework` verdict
74	and instead park the plan in this state; a human CLI command
75	(`megaplan verify-human --plan X --criterion C --pass`) flips it to
76	`done`. Catches: the end-to-end lifecycle including "who actually
77	confirmed". Misses: still requires the tagging from (a) upstream; adds
78	a new state machine branch that has to be taught to status, batch
79	runners, and loop-init. Medium-to-large cost; meaningful worker
80	contract change (review must emit a new verdict `awaiting_human` in
81	addition to `approved` / `needs_rework`).
82	
83	### (d) Two-array schema split (machine_criteria, human_criteria)
84	The plan author writes two explicit arrays. Review evaluates only
85	`machine_criteria`. `human_criteria` go into the PR description or a
86	checklist file and never touch review. Catches: the conflation directly
87	at the schema level; makes the author's two audiences structurally
88	separate. Misses: authors who lazily shove everything into one bucket;
89	the expensive-machine-gate case. Small cost; but a large change in
90	authoring ergonomics — existing specs break unless we fall back to
91	treating `success_criteria` as `machine_criteria`.
92	
93	### (e) Reviewer self-assessment of verifiability
94	Let the reviewer return, per criterion, one of
95	`pass | fail | waived_unverifiable | waived_info`. Today's `waived`
96	covers both `info` priority and unverifiable; split that. The reviewer
97	decides, not the author. Catches: the M0 case without touching spec
98	authoring; the reviewer is usually in the best position to know what
99	it cannot verify. Misses: authors still paste nonsense criteria; the
100	loop wastes a whole execute pass before the reviewer shrugs; also
101	creates a new gaming vector where `waived_unverifiable` means "I didn't
102	try hard enough." Low cost in isolation.
103	
104	### (f) Worker capability profile + static criterion linter
105	New-for-this-proposal. Each worker declares a *capability profile* — a
106	small structured blob listing what it can execute (`run_shell`,
107	`run_node_tests`, `read_build_output`, `observe_browser`,
108	`observe_runtime_logs`, ...). At plan-finalize time, each success
109	criterion is parsed by a linter prompt that maps it to the capabilities
110	it needs. A criterion whose required capabilities are a subset of the
111	configured worker's profile is `machine_verifiable: true`. Everything
112	else is `machine_verifiable: false` and is automatically treated as a
113	human-deferred criterion. The author does not tag anything; the
114	harness computes it.
115	
116	## Recommendation: a fused (a)+(b)+(e), with (f) as the v0.18 follow-up
117	
118	Pick option (a) as the storage model, option (b) as the upstream defense,
119	and option (e) as the downstream safety net. Deliver all three in v0.17.0.
120	Defer (f) because capability profiles are a much bigger design problem —
121	they couple to worker contracts, the trusted-container env, and the
122	hermes worker, and we do not need them to fix the immediate pain. (c) is
123	tempting but adds a state machine branch for a problem that `waived`
124	already models well; reject. (d) forces existing specs to break; reject.
125	
126	Why fuse three rather than pick one: each option on its own has a
127	failure mode the other two cover.
128	
129	- (a) alone: author forgets to tag -> reviewer still fails. (e) catches.
130	- (b) alone: audit passes because criteria *look* machine-verifiable
131	  (e.g., "baseline counts captured" reads as machine-checkable but
132	  requires a browser). (a) plus (e) catch at review time.
133	- (e) alone: reviewer correctly waives, but the author never learns
134	  the spec was malformed; the next milestone repeats the mistake. (b)
135	  surfaces the problem at authorship.
136	
137	The three-layer structure mirrors megaplan's existing philosophy (plan
138	gate filters → execute audit → review verdict), just applied to the
139	verifiability axis.
140	
141	## Implementation sketch
142	
143	### Schema changes (`megaplan/schemas.py`)
144	`plan.json` and `finalize.json` success_criteria items gain:
145	```
146	"verified_by": {"type": "string", "enum": ["container", "human", "mixed"], "default": "container"}
147	"verification_hint": {"type": "string"}  // optional, free-text: "requires running browser", etc.
148	```
149	Review-output criteria gain a new `pass` enum value:
150	```
151	"pass": {"type": "string", "enum": ["pass", "fail", "waived", "waived_unverifiable", "deferred_human"]}
152	```
153	Existing `waived` is preserved for `info` priority. Missing `verified_by`
154	defaults to `container` — every existing plan keeps working unchanged.
155	
156	### Plan-phase audit (option b)
157	New file: `megaplan/verifiability.py`. Exposes `audit_criteria(state, criteria)`
158	which runs a single-shot worker call (same pattern as `run_gate_checks`)
159	asking: "for each criterion, is it reachable by a worker with capabilities
160	`run_shell`, `read_files`, `git`, but no browser, no human hands, no manual
161	observation? Return `container`, `human`, or `mixed` and one-line
162	rationale." Results are written to `plan_dir/verifiability.json` and
163	surfaced as advisory critique flags with category `verifiability`. The
164	author (or gate) can override by explicitly setting `verified_by` on the
165	criterion — the audit never overwrites an explicit tag, only fills in
166	missing ones.
167	
168	Runs after `finalize`, before `execute` starts. Keeps the
169	critique→gate→revise loop as the resolution surface — no new state.
170	
171	### Review-phase handling (option e)
172	`megaplan/prompts/review.py` gains two rules:
173	- If criterion's `verified_by == "human"`: reviewer MUST mark
174	  `pass: "deferred_human"` and MUST NOT count it toward the
175	  `needs_rework` tally. `review_verdict = approved` is valid even if
176	  every human criterion is deferred.
177	- If reviewer finds a `container`-tagged criterion it genuinely cannot
178	  verify (e.g., the tooling isn't present in this environment), it
179	  marks `pass: "waived_unverifiable"` with an evidence sentence naming
180	  *what* it couldn't run, and surfaces a flag `REVIEW-UNVERIFIABLE-NNN`.
181	  A `must` criterion going `waived_unverifiable` is a soft block — it
182	  downgrades verdict to `needs_rework` only if `>= N` of them occur
183	  (configurable; default 1 for `must`, infinity for `should`). This
184	  prevents the M0 cascade.
185	
186	Merging logic (`_merge_review_verdicts` at `handlers.py:1421`) must learn
187	the new enum values and stop treating them as `fail`.
188	
189	### CLI
190	- `megaplan audit-verifiability --plan X` — run the audit on demand.
191	- `megaplan status` shows counts: "3 container / 2 human / 0 mixed".
192	- `megaplan verify-human --plan X --criterion "Baseline doc captured"
193	  --pass --evidence "Confirmed 5 components × 3 interactions in doc
194	  at commit abc123"` — records the human confirmation in
195	  `plan_dir/human_verifications.json`. Review re-runs treat these as
196	  resolved. (Optional for v0.17.0; falls back to "human flips state
197	  with a comment" if we want to defer.)
198	
199	### Migration
200	- Existing plans without `verified_by`: default `container`. Same
201	  behavior as today.
202	- Existing plans in `awaiting_review` / `needs_rework` for the M0-class
203	  reason: add a one-shot retrofit script that parses the review verdict
204	  and re-tags criteria whose failure evidence includes phrases like
205	  "cannot verify", "no browser", "requires manual". Offered as a CLI
206	  tool, not automatic.
207	- Tests: add fixtures under `tests/fixtures/verifiability/` that mirror
208	  M0 — container-only execution, spec with mixed gates, expected
209	  `approved` verdict with deferrals.
210	
211	### Out of scope (v0.17.0)
212	- Worker capability profiles (option f). Deferred to v0.18.0 when we
213	  re-examine worker contracts wholesale.
214	- Schema-level split into two arrays (option d). Tag is sufficient.
215	- Auto-flipping `awaiting_human_verification` based on PR comments or
216	  GitHub checks. Manual CLI confirmation only.
217	- Teaching loop mode about deferrals. v0.17.0 treats a plan with any
218	  `deferred_human` criteria as "done for autonomous purposes"; loops
219	  continue to the next plan.
220	
221	## Success criteria (verifiable)
222	
223	- `megaplan init` accepts plans whose `success_criteria[].verified_by`
224	  is `container`, `human`, or `mixed`. Missing field defaults to
225	  `container` — asserted by schema round-trip test.
226	- `megaplan audit-verifiability --plan X` produces
227	  `verifiability.json` with one entry per criterion and exits 0.
228	- A fixture plan with a `verified_by: human` criterion runs through
229	  review and yields `review_verdict: approved`, `pass: deferred_human`
230	  for that criterion, and no `rework_items` entries sourced from it.
231	- A fixture plan with an undetectable-by-container criterion (e.g.,
232	  "browser renders without warnings") and `verified_by` unset triggers
233	  a verifiability flag at audit time, category `verifiability`.
234	- Reviewer emitting `pass: waived_unverifiable` on a `must` criterion
235	  still routes to `needs_rework` (soft block preserved); emitting it
236	  on a `should` criterion does not.
237	- `megaplan verify-human --plan X --criterion C --pass --evidence E`
238	  writes `human_verifications.json` and, on a re-review, the entry is
239	  honored: verdict stays `approved`, pass flips from `deferred_human`
240	  to `pass`.
241	- Existing test suite passes unchanged — all legacy plans default to
242	  `container` and behave exactly as before.
243	- `pyproject.toml` version is `0.17.0`; CHANGELOG has the v0.17.0 entry.
244	
245	## Edge cases — and answers
246	
247	- **Mixed human + machine gates in one plan.** Supported first-class;
248	  review emits both `pass` and `deferred_human` verdicts; `approved` is
249	  possible when all machine `must` criteria pass and all human `must`
250	  criteria are deferred. The plan status becomes `approved_with_deferrals`
251	  in `status` output — a label, not a new state.
252	- **Worker identity changes mid-plan** (claude plans, codex executes,
253	  hermes reviews). Capability is conservatively the intersection across
254	  the executing + reviewing workers. The audit runs with the *executor's*
255	  profile; review with its own. If review has fewer capabilities than
256	  execute, `waived_unverifiable` can still fire at review time — this is
257	  correct: review couldn't verify, regardless of whether execute could.
258	- **Machine-verifiable but expensive** (full e2e, 30-minute build).
259	  These are `verified_by: container` but get a `verification_hint` of
260	  `"expensive"`. Not handled in v0.17.0 — a future `verified_by: container_slow`
261	  tag would let the harness choose to defer them in CI-gated contexts.
262	  Explicitly out of scope now; the hint is present so we do not have to
263	  re-migrate schemas later.
264	- **Gaming: author marks everything `human` to skip checks.** Three
265	  defenses. (1) The verifiability audit runs regardless of the author's
266	  tag; if the audit says a criterion *is* container-reachable, that
267	  appears as a flag at gate time even when the author claimed `human`.
268	  (2) `megaplan status` surfaces the container/human ratio; a plan with
269	  7 human and 0 container criteria is visually anomalous to the human
270	  operator. (3) Review's `waived_unverifiable` counter still applies —
271	  marking something `human` does not exempt it from the soft block if
272	  review independently finds the claim is machine-checkable. We do not
273	  try to make gaming impossible; we make it visible.
274	
275	## Authorship ergonomics
276	
277	Today a spec author writes one list of bullets. Under v0.17.0 they write
278	the same list, and most criteria default to `container` implicitly. The
279	only new burden is tagging the criteria they already know a machine
280	cannot verify. To lower even that burden:
281	
282	- The `megaplan init` prompt gains a one-line nudge: "Any success
283	  criterion that requires human observation (browser, device, QA
284	  confirmation) should set `verified_by: human`."
285	- A scaffolding command `megaplan new-spec --template milestone` writes
286	  a template markdown file with two example criteria pre-filled, one
287	  per `verified_by` value, so the author sees the shape.
288	- The verifiability audit's output is itself the teaching signal: if
289	  the author forgets, the flag surfaces with rationale and the author
290	  learns the pattern on the next spec.
291	
292	The system is strictly *easier* to get right: the failure mode goes
293	from "ship to a container, burn a run, fail review opaquely" to
294	"critique emits a flag at plan time, author adjusts tag or rewrites
295	criterion." The only way v0.17.0 is harder than today is if the author
296	wants to preserve the current behavior of pasting CLAUDE.md bullets
297	into the criteria block — which is exactly the behavior we are trying
298	to make uncomfortable.
299	
300	## Branch
301	`gate-verifiability` off main.
302	
303	## Working directory
304	/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/megaplan
305

1	v0.15.0 — doc mode (metaplan): plan-as-output instead of code-as-output
2	
3	## Goal
4	Introduce a `--mode doc` (a.k.a. metaplan mode) where the executor produces a
5	structured plan document instead of code changes. Same harness, same phases,
6	same flag/gate machinery — only the executor's tool surface and output schema
7	change. Use case: plan-of-plans, design docs, RFCs, milestone breakdowns,
8	research write-ups. Anything where the deliverable is words on disk, not a diff.
9	
10	## Motivation
11	Today megaplan only knows how to ship code — execute writes files in the repo,
12	audit compares claimed paths against `git status`, review measures success
13	against criteria like "tsc clean" and "tests pass." When the artifact we want
14	is a plan document (e.g. the `state_management_refactor_plan.md` we just wrote
15	by hand, or the per-milestone idea files I'm seeding into `~/Documents/reigh-megaplan-dev/ideas/`),
16	megaplan can't help — its critique/gate/review loop is tuned for code.
17	
18	If we add doc mode, the whole prep → plan → critique → gate → revise loop
19	applies to thinking work too: the gate forces resolution of every blocking
20	critique flag against the document; review checks the doc against success
21	criteria. The model gets the same anti-rubber-stamp pressure on its writing
22	that it gets on its code.
23	
24	## What stays the same
25	- All phases (prep, plan, critique, gate, revise, finalize, execute, review).
26	- Robustness levels (light/standard/heavy).
27	- Flag taxonomy, dispute/accept_tradeoff resolution, rubber-stamp checks.
28	- Override commands (force-proceed, abort, replan, add-note).
29	- Session/rollout management, trusted-container env, batch execution.
30	- Critique prompts at the plan level — critiquing a plan is the same activity
31	  whether the plan ships code or ships a doc.
32	
33	## What varies per phase
34	
35	### init
36	- New flag: `--mode {code,doc}` (default `code`).
37	- Mode persists in plan meta (`plan.json` → `mode: "doc"`). All later phases
38	  read it from there.
39	- New flag: `--output <path>` for doc mode. Required. Path is relative to
40	  project_dir. Single output file — multi-file docs are out of scope for v0.15.
41	
42	### prep
43	- Unchanged for code mode.
44	- For doc mode: prep gathers research instead of repo orientation. The prep
45	  prompt is repointed to ask "what sources, prior art, related docs should
46	  inform this document?" — sense-check items become "did you read X?" rather
47	  than "did you find the relevant module?"
48	
49	### plan
50	- Plan output schema is unchanged at the top level (steps, tasks, success
51	  criteria, sense checks).
52	- Tasks in doc mode have a different shape under the hood: instead of
53	  `files_changed: [paths]`, they have `sections_written: [section_ids]`.
54	  The plan-step prompt enumerates the sections of the target document
55	  (introduction, problem statement, proposed solution, milestones, …) and
56	  the executor's job is to write each section.
57	
58	### critique
59	- Same machinery. Critique flags target plan structure, success-criteria
60	  calibration, scope creep — identical to code mode.
61	- Add a category `doc-quality` (alongside `code-quality`, `security`, etc.)
62	  for flags about clarity, audience-fit, missing rationale, undefended
63	  claims. Doc-mode critiques skew this way; code-mode critiques rarely use it.
64	
65	### gate
66	- Identical. The gate doesn't care what the executor will produce; it judges
67	  the plan's readiness.
68	
69	### revise → finalize
70	- Identical.
71	
72	### execute
73	- This is the biggest change.
74	- Tool surface: codex/claude is told it's authoring a document. Its only
75	  filesystem tool is "write to the configured output path." File creation
76	  outside that path is rejected upstream.
77	- Output schema: `task_updates[].files_changed` is replaced with
78	  `task_updates[].sections_written: [section_id]`. Tasks have status
79	  done/skipped/blocked as today.
80	- The executor returns the rendered section text, not a diff. The harness
81	  assembles sections in plan-order into the output file at the end of the
82	  batch. (This is how we avoid concurrent writers fighting over the same
83	  file across batches.)
84	- Per-batch behavior unchanged: each batch covers some tasks, writes its
85	  evidence JSON, transitions to the next.
86	
87	### audit (post-execute)
88	- For code mode: today's `validate_execution_evidence` (git status diff,
89	  path normalization, sense-check acks).
90	- For doc mode: replace the git-status comparison with:
91	  - "all sections in the plan are present in the output file"
92	  - "no sections in the output file are unclaimed by any task"
93	  - "output file exists and is non-empty"
94	  - "executor's claimed `sections_written` match what the harness assembled"
95	- Sense-check acknowledgment validation is unchanged.
96	
97	### review
98	- Code mode: today's review (tests pass, types clean, success criteria met).
99	- Doc mode: review reads the output file and judges it against the success
100	  criteria. `must` criteria become statements like "the doc names every
101	  blocking risk" rather than "tsc clean." Review's prompt is reworded to
102	  treat the deliverable as text, not a working system.
103	- Same priority machinery (must/should/info), same `needs_rework` loop.
104	
105	## Wiring details
106	
107	### Mode plumbing
108	- `plan.json` gains `mode: "code" | "doc"` and (for doc mode) `output_path`.
109	- Workers receive mode in their context dict.
110	- Prompt files split by mode: `prompts/prep_doc.py`, `prompts/execute_doc.py`,
111	  `prompts/review_doc.py`. Other prompts stay shared.
112	- `evaluation.validate_execution_evidence` branches on mode at the top.
113	
114	### Output schema
115	- New `schemas/execution_doc.json` mirrors `schemas/execution.json` but with
116	  `sections_written` instead of `files_changed`.
117	- `merge.py` validation accepts the doc schema when mode is doc.
118	
119	### Section assembly
120	- New `megaplan/doc_assembly.py`: takes the per-batch executor outputs,
121	  orders sections by plan position, writes the assembled file at finalize-end.
122	- Idempotent: running execute twice on the same plan replaces the file.
123	  No partial writes — assemble in a temp file, then atomic rename.
124	
125	## CLI shape
126	
127	```
128	megaplan init --project-dir . --mode doc \
129	              --output docs/state_management_refactor_plan.md \
130	              "Plan a 6-week refactor of state management..."
131	```
132	
133	Everything else is unchanged. `megaplan status` shows `mode: doc` and
134	`output_path` in the summary.
135	
136	## Out of scope (v0.15.0)
137	- Multi-file doc output (one plan → one file in v0.15).
138	- Mixed-mode plans (a plan that ships both code and a doc).
139	- Doc-mode-aware loop-init / loop-execute. Loop mode stays code-only for now.
140	- Migrating existing code-mode prompts to use the new schema branching —
141	  add the branch, don't rewrite working prompts.
142	
143	## Migration / compatibility
144	- Existing plans with no `mode` field default to `code`. No retroactive change.
145	- Existing tests pass unchanged (they all hit code mode).
146	- New tests cover: doc-mode plan init, doc execute writes the file, audit
147	  catches missing sections, audit catches sections not in plan, review
148	  judges doc against criteria.
149	
150	## Success criteria (verifiable)
151	- `megaplan init --mode doc --output X "..."` produces a plan with `mode: doc`.
152	- Running the full loop on a doc-mode plan produces a non-empty file at the
153	  configured output path.
154	- Audit rejects an executor that claims a section not in the plan.
155	- Audit rejects an executor that skips a section without marking the task
156	  blocked/skipped.
157	- Review with a `must` criterion phrased about the doc's content can fail
158	  the doc and trigger needs_rework.
159	- All existing code-mode tests pass.
160	- pyproject.toml version is "0.15.0", CHANGELOG has the v0.15.0 entry.
161	
162	## Branch
163	`doc-mode-metaplan` off main.
164	
165	## Working directory
166	/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/megaplan
167
```

1	v0.14.0 — strict flag-resolution at the gate
2	
3	## Goal
4	Remove the silent implicit-acceptance of unresolved blocking flags when the gate recommends PROCEED. Make the gate either resolve every blocking flag explicitly, or pick ITERATE / ESCALATE. Reject rubber-stamp rationale on accept_tradeoff actions, not just on dispute actions.
5	
6	## Motivation
7	The current gate logic (v0.13) has two related problems:
8	1. The gate prompt tells the agent "you may resolve at most 3 flags explicitly per gate call. Any remaining blocking flags are implicitly accepted as tradeoffs if you recommend PROCEED." (prompts/gate.py, around lines 105-114)
9	2. The handler enforces this by silently auto-marking unresolved blocking flags as accept_tradeoff (handlers.py, around lines 621-635 inside _apply_gate_outcome).
10	3. The rubber-stamp check (handlers.py around lines 600-607) only validates dispute.evidence — it accepts any accept_tradeoff.rationale including boilerplate.
11	
12	Net effect: a gate PROCEED can ship with 5 unresolved blocking flags, silently auto-accepted, with zero resistance from the system. The human reviewing the PR sees them in accepted_tradeoffs but the agent was never forced to reason about each one.
13	
14	## Exact changes
15	
16	### Change 1: prompts/gate.py
17	Replace the block that currently reads roughly:
18	  "You may resolve at most 3 flags explicitly per gate call. Any remaining
19	  blocking flags are implicitly accepted as tradeoffs if you recommend PROCEED.
20	  If a flag is structurally unresolvable (e.g., references infrastructure
21	  outside the repo), you should still PROCEED — do not loop indefinitely
22	  on flags that cannot be addressed."
23	
24	with strict language:
25	  "If you recommend PROCEED, you MUST provide a flag_resolutions entry for
26	  every blocking flag. There is no implicit acceptance. If you cannot
27	  resolve every blocking flag, choose ITERATE (send back for revision)
28	  or ESCALATE (human intervention needed). Structurally unresolvable flags
29	  (infrastructure outside the repo, product decision required) are ESCALATE,
30	  not PROCEED with a non-answer.
31	
32	  For each blocking flag:
33	  - dispute: critique is factually wrong. Evidence must cite specific
34	    file/line/doc — generic statements like 'handled correctly' are invalid.
35	  - accept_tradeoff: concern is real but accepted as a known limitation.
36	    Rationale must be specific to this flag — 'acceptable within scope'
37	    is not valid rationale."
38	
39	Keep the existing example JSON, but update it to show explicit resolutions for every listed blocking flag (not just a subset).
40	
41	### Change 2: megaplan/handlers.py _apply_gate_outcome
42	Replace the silent implicit-acceptance block (the "Implicitly accept remaining blocking flags as tradeoffs" branch around lines 621-635) with:
43	
44	  - If PROCEED and blocking_unresolved is non-empty:
45	    - If this is the first attempt for this iteration: reprompt the gate worker once, with the missing flag IDs listed in the new prompt. The existing worker machinery should support this (see _run_worker and the refreshed flag).
46	    - If reprompt also returns blocking_unresolved: force-downgrade recommendation to ITERATE. Mutate gate_summary in place so the artifact reflects the downgrade. Append to gate_summary["rationale"]: " [Auto-downgraded from PROCEED: N blocking flag(s) not resolved after reprompt]"
47	    - Return next_step = "revise".
48	  - Do NOT call update_flags_after_gate with implicit resolutions for unresolved flags. Remove the implicit_resolutions list entirely.
49	
50	Persist a marker in state or the gate artifact so we can tell whether reprompt already happened this iteration. Either a field on gate_summary (e.g., `reprompted: true`) or a key in state meta. Pick whichever is less invasive.
51	
52	### Change 3: megaplan/handlers.py rubber-stamp check extension
53	In the loop around lines 597-608 that processes resolutions:
54	
55	  - Keep the existing dispute check (skip if evidence is missing or is_rubber_stamp returns True).
56	  - Add a matching check for accept_tradeoff: skip if rationale is missing or is_rubber_stamp(rationale, strict=True) returns True. A skipped accept_tradeoff means the flag is treated as unresolved and falls through to the Change 2 logic.
57	
58	### Change 4: tests
59	Update existing gate tests:
60	- Test that a PROCEED with 3 resolutions out of 5 blocking flags triggers a reprompt, not silent acceptance.
61	- Test that a PROCEED still missing flags after reprompt is auto-downgraded to ITERATE, with the appended rationale.
62	- Test that an accept_tradeoff with rubber-stamp rationale ("acceptable", "fine as is") is rejected.
63	- Test that an accept_tradeoff with concrete rationale passes.
64	- Test that PROCEED with every blocking flag resolved (no reprompt needed) still works end-to-end.
65	
66	Remove any existing test that asserts the implicit-acceptance behavior (that was testing a bug).
67	
68	### Change 5: version bump
69	- pyproject.toml: version "0.13.0" -> "0.14.0".
70	- CHANGELOG.md: new v0.14.0 entry summarizing the above.
71	
72	## Out of scope (explicitly NOT doing in v0.14.0)
73	- Do not add a separate per-flag resolve phase.
74	- Do not add scaffolding-level recurrence counters or divergence detectors — the gate agent already sees iteration history via gate_signals and can reason about recurrence on its own.
75	- Do not add severity-gated auto-ITERATE rules beyond what the existing logic covers.
76	- Do not change the flag severity taxonomy (blocking = significant + likely-significant; noted = everything else).
77	- Do not change the override commands (force-proceed, abort, replan, add-note).
78	- Do not touch the gate signals computation, preflight checks, or worker infrastructure.
79	
80	## Branch + commit hygiene
81	- Create branch `gate-strict-flag-resolution` off main.
82	- One commit for the code change, one for the test update is fine, or a single atomic commit — reviewer preference.
83	- Commit message must reference v0.14.0 and summarize the behavior change.
84	- Open a PR on GitHub against main when done. Do not auto-merge.

89	- Running the existing test fixture that simulates a gate PROCEED with unresolved flags produces an ITERATE downgrade (not silent acceptance).
90	- pyproject.toml version is "0.14.0".
91	- CHANGELOG.md has the new entry.

## Executive summary

The proposal is directionally right but operationally overbuilt. It correctly rejects the shallow "just add a tag" reading and names three real frames (plan/review gate conflation, missing authorship feedback, underspecified `waived`), but its fused (a)+(b)+(e) solution is a compromise that partially solves each without fully solving any. Four severe problems: (1) `deferred_human` is a silent accumulator — v0.17.0 explicitly does not teach loop mode about deferrals and makes `megaplan verify-human` optional, so in the solo-operator model deferred gates will accumulate unchecked, which is strictly worse than today's loud failure. (2) The three anti-gaming defenses for `verified_by: human` don't actually compose — the audit uses the same natural-language reasoning as review, the status-ratio visibility is invisible in loop mode, and the soft-block counter doesn't fire on author-tagged `human` criteria. (3) The real root is missing *executor capability contract*, not missing tags — option (f), deferred, is the only thing that attacks root; shipping (a)+(b)+(e) first mortgages schema surface. (4) Walking M0 through the proposed system, the audit catches the easy criteria (overlay toggle) but misses the hard one (self-contradictory baseline doc spec), so the motivating case isn't actually fixed. Recommend revising: drop the `verified_by` schema field and new enum values, keep only the audit but move it pre-critique and make it binding, and commit to a v0.18.0 capability-profile release.

You are doing an adversarial read of a proposed elegant solution to a megaplan harness problem. Your ONLY job is to find what this solution LOSES compared to alternatives — be a skeptic looking for regressions, gaps, and ways this is worse than what it replaces.

## Context — read these three docs in order

1. **The motivating failure**: `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh-megaplan-dev/ideas/M0-render-telemetry.txt` (the spec that got stuck because codex-in-a-container can't verify browser-required gates).
2. **Original proposal**: `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/megaplan/idea-gate-verifiability.txt` — v0.17.0 three-part fix: `verified_by` tags on criteria, a post-finalize audit module, splitting `waived` into `deferred_human` + `waived_unverifiable`.
3. **Critique of that proposal**: `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/megaplan/idea-gate-verifiability-critique.txt` — says the proposal is "directionally right, operationally overbuilt" with four severe issues; recommends dropping the tag/waived work, keeping only the audit (pre-critique and binding), and committing to v0.18.0 being the capability-profile release.

## The proposal you are evaluating

After reading proposal + critique, we converged on one unified idea: **capability matching**. Here is the full shape (treat this as the spec under review):

```yaml
# worker config — small, hand-written, rarely changes
workers:
  codex_container:
    verifies: [read_repo, run_tsc, run_vitest, parse_diff, grep_bundle]
  human_reviewer:
    verifies: [drive_browser, inspect_runtime_ui, subjective_judgment,
               verify_render_counts, verify_physics]
```

```yaml
# each success_criterion gets ONE new optional field: requires: [capability, ...]
- criterion: "ImageLightbox opens with ≤5 renders"
  priority: must
  requires: [drive_browser, verify_render_counts]
```

**Mechanics:**
- **Plan phase**: for every `must` criterion, assert `requires ⊆ union(worker.verifies)` across configured workers. If not, fail loud pre-execution.
- **Review phase**: reviewer evaluates only criteria whose `requires` it can verify. Others route to a `pending-human queue`.
- `done` is blocked until `megaplan verify-human --plan X` clears the queue.
- **Solo-dev**: if `human_reviewer` isn't configured, human-required criteria are rejected at plan time — you literally can't author a stuck spec.
- **Migration**: criteria without `requires` default to `[]` (match any worker) → existing behavior preserved.

The pitch: one concept (capability matching) replaces three subsystems (tags + audit + waived-split); no new terminal state (wait, except `awaiting_human_verify`); no gaming surface because capabilities live in worker config, not spec metadata; fails loud at plan time.

## Your task

Find what this proposal **loses** versus:
- The v0.17.0 original three-part fix.
- The critique's "just a binding pre-critique audit" alternative.
- The existing v0.16.x system with no changes at all.

Specifically stress these angles:

1. **Does capability naming actually work?** The vocabulary is open-ended (`drive_browser`, `verify_render_counts`, `verify_physics`). Who maintains it? Does every new criterion invent a new capability? Does this become a tagging treadmill?
2. **Plan-time hard failure is LOUD**. Is that always good? What's lost when a plan *can't be drafted* because capabilities aren't configured, versus the current world where it at least runs and produces code you can inspect?
3. **The `pending-human queue`** — is it better than the critique's concern about silent accumulators? Or does it become a mailbox nobody reads? Who sends the reminder?
4. **Migration default `requires: []` preserves behavior** — but it also means existing specs get ZERO benefit without a rewrite. Is that worse or better than the v0.17 proposal's default-to-container which at least tries to infer?
5. **Edge cases the v0.17 critique flagged**: self-contradictory specs (like M0's "non-HMR dev-built" requirement), mid-plan worker swap, expensive-but-machine gates. Does capability matching catch these, or do they still slip through?
6. **Grain-size mismatch**: capabilities are coarse (e.g. `drive_browser`), criteria are fine (e.g. "≤5 renders on lightbox open"). One capability covers many criteria. What happens when a capability is *partially* present — e.g. a worker can drive a browser but not inspect React internals? Does the system collapse to binary when it shouldn't?
7. **Worker discovery**: how does the plan phase know which workers are configured? Is this static config, or does it inspect the environment (claude auth? codex auth? human operator plugged in?) Who decides `human_reviewer` is "available"?
8. **Gaming revisited**: the proposal claims no gaming surface because capabilities are worker config. But a motivated spec author can still fail to declare `requires: [drive_browser]` on a criterion that needs it, and the system won't know. Is this actually solved, or just moved?
9. **Integration with `review.py`**: the current reviewer evaluates all criteria in one pass. Does splitting evaluation by capability force a multi-pass review? What's the cost?
10. **What about implicit capabilities**? "Verify that ImageLightbox opens" requires browser AND a running app AND test data. Capability lists can't express "X AND Y AND Z" naturally — they're flat sets. Does this break on composite requirements?

## Deliverable

Write to `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/megaplan/idea-gate-verifiability-losses.txt`. Same dense-prose style as the other idea files. Structure:

1. **One-paragraph verdict**: does the capability-matching proposal actually win, and if so by how much? Be specific. No hedging.
2. **Concrete losses**, ranked. For each: what's lost, what scenario it bites in, what it would take to recover. Not generic "complexity" — specific failure modes with file paths / CLI interactions / YAML snippets.
3. **What capability matching solves that the other proposals don't** — the honest case for it. Keep this balanced; you're looking for losses but shouldn't be dishonest about wins.
4. **Recommendation**: ship capability-matching as-is? Ship with specific modifications? Ship the critique's simpler audit-only path? Or gather more data? Commit.

2-3 pages dense prose, matching the other idea files.

## Depth bar

The proposal already looks elegant. Your job is to find what it costs. If you conclude nothing substantial is lost, say so with evidence. If you find a real loss, be specific enough that someone could patch the proposal to cover it.
